extracted.intended_audience: computational linguistics / NLP researchers and practitioners working on sentiment analysis (lexicon-based methods)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating lexicon-based systems that compute semantic orientation (polarity and strength) of words/phrases and aggregate them for polarity classification of texts; includes dictionary construction, handling of valence shifters, negation, irrealis, and evaluation across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity classification task
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of assigning a positive or negative label to a text that captures the text’s opinion towards its main subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO-CAL is applied to this task and evaluated on consistency across domains and on completely unseen data; performance measured by accuracy on held-out corpora (e.g., movie reviews, Epinions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of prior polarity and numeric SO values
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual words have a prior polarity (semantic orientation independent of context) and that semantic orientation can be expressed as a numerical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many lexicon-based approaches adopt this; SO values in SO-CAL are numeric (hand-ranked on a −5 to +5 scale) and averaged across likely interpretations when senses are not disambiguated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary creation method (manual vs automatic / semi-automatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries can be created manually (hand-tagging) or automatically/semi-automatically (seed words, corpus co-occurrence, Web counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatically created dictionaries can find novel words but may be unstable (Google-based methods unstable); manual creation (hand-tagging from development corpus) yields reliable entries but requires effort; a committee review and Mechanical Turk checks can improve consistency and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of speech coverage (adjectives, nouns, verbs, adverbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include open-class words beyond adjectives; create separate dictionaries for adjectives, nouns, verbs, and adverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early work focused on adjectives, but nouns/verbs/adverbs carry SO too; SO-CAL uses separate noun, verb, and adverb dictionaries (and an adjective dictionary) with hand-ranked SO values.

rubrics_metrics.name: SO value scale and neutrality treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a signed numeric scale (SO values from +5 to −5) with neutral/zero words excluded from dictionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values reflect both prior polarity and strength; when one sense is uncommon the averaged value is used; neutral words (0) are excluded from the active dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemmatization and form-insensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemmatize nouns and verbs and ignore morphological form (singular/plural, tense) when looking up SO values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After stripping endings, perform dictionary look-up; this avoids treating inflected forms as distinct entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-word expressions and precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Support multi-word entries (regular-expression-like) and give multi-word entries precedence over single-word entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: phrasal verbs like 'fall apart' or intensifier phrases like 'a little bit'; multi-word matches override single-word SO values (e.g., 'act funny' negative despite 'funny' positive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensification modeled with percentage modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Model intensifiers and downtoners as percentage modifiers applied multiplicatively to the SO value of the target word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each intensifying word has a percent (e.g., very +25%, somewhat −30%); modifiers apply recursively from closest to the SO-valued word; this captures both modifier strength and dependence on the item being modified (e.g., 'truly fantastic' vs 'truly okay').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-lexical intensifiers (caps, exclamation, discourse connectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat features such as all-capital letters, exclamation marks, and discourse connective 'but' as intensifiers affecting SO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These genre-specific signals are included in the intensifier dictionary or handled as special intensification mechanisms (e.g., '... but the movie was GREAT!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectival intensifiers vs adjective SO entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adjectives act as intensifiers when modifying nouns rather than as independent SO-bearing items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a separate adjectival intensifier dictionary so when such adjectives appear adjacent to SO-valued nouns they are treated as modifiers (e.g., 'total failure' treats 'total' as an intensifier rather than independent SO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation handling: scope detection and two negation models
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation requires (a) detecting scope (where the negator applies) and (b) deciding how to change SO (switch/polarity flip or polarity shift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO-CAL implements backward search for negators up to clause boundaries or using skip-lists tailored by part of speech (conservative approach used). Two negation models discussed: switch negation (flip sign) and shift negation (shift toward opposite polarity by fixed amount, e.g., 4); authors prefer polarity shift as more pragmatically realistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation scope search strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches for negation scope: (1) look backwards until a clause boundary marker; (2) look backwards while words/tags are in a backward-search skip list (different lists per part of speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conservative skip-list approach (allowing some tokens to be skipped but stopping at others) worked better in experiments and is used in SO-CAL; full parsing is an alternative but slower and ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation interaction with intensifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation interacts with intensifiers and must handle compound expressions (e.g., 'not very good') correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include flipping both adjective and intensifier or using polarity shift; polarity-flip models can produce counterintuitive results ('not very good' more negative than 'not good'), so polarity shift or flipping intensifier signs may be preferable with tuned parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrealis blocking (ignore SO in non-factive contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignore semantic-orientation values for words within the scope of irrealis markers (non-factive contexts), because they may not reflect the author's stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrealis markers include modals, conditional markers (if), NPIs like any, certain intensional verbs (expect, doubt), questions, and quoted words; SO-CAL currently ignores SO inside such scopes rather than flipping polarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of negative polarity items (NPIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle NPIs (any, anything, ever, at all) primarily as irrealis blockers rather than negators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPIs often occur in nonveridical contexts; treating them as irrealis blockers reduces SO values in such contexts; in some cases searching for NPI may be more effective than searching for explicit negators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage vs noise tradeoff in dictionary size
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger dictionaries (greater coverage) are not necessarily better because including rarer or descriptive vocabulary can introduce noise and reduce performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding words found in held-out texts decreased performance in experiments (e.g., adding low-frequency sentiment words dropped accuracy); balance coverage with noise control and consider genre descriptiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop-word lists associated with POS-specific dictionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate stop-word lists with each POS dictionary to exclude tokens that are tagged as that POS but should not be treated as SO-bearing (e.g., more, much tagged as adjectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop-lists prevent misinterpretation due to POS tagging errors and common non-SO tokens; maintain per-dictionary stop lists (adjective, noun, verb, adverb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic derivation of adverb dictionary with manual corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct adverb entries by mapping -ly adverbs to corresponding adjective entries, with manual corrections for mismatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method yields good coverage but some adverbs (e.g., 'essentially') require manual adjustment when meaning diverges from adjective base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle grammatical metaphor and POS-specific SO differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that related forms (verb vs noun) can have different SO values (e.g., exaggerate −1 vs exaggeration −2) and grammatical metaphor (noun referring to action) can add negativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign different SO values per lemma+POS; treat noun/verb separately rather than assuming same polarity/strength across forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation methods for document SO
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate individual word/phrase SO values into a single document score; earlier versions used add-and-average (sum SO values divided by number of adjectives), whereas later versions use more sophisticated weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple aggregate-and-average is a baseline but may be improved by weighting contributions (e.g., taking intensifiers, relevance, multi-word precedence, and POS into account); relevance and genre should influence aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary validation and reliability checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate dictionaries against other resources and human judgments; use committee review and crowd-sourced checks to ensure consistency and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO-CAL dictionaries were hand-ranked and reviewed by a committee; Mechanical Turk was used to compare and confirm values; compare against existing lexicons (General Inquirer, SentiWordNet, Maryland) to assess robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate robustness across domains and unseen data
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure system performance across multiple domains and on completely unseen datasets to assess domain independence and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO-CAL experiments show consistent performance across domains; compare performance to supervised classifiers which often drop when transferred across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle descriptive/genre-specific signals separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that descriptive vocabulary (genre-specific terms) may not reflect sentiment and can bias classifiers or lexicons trained on domain data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address descriptive noise (e.g., movie-review specific tokens like 'sequel', '2', 'tv') through genre-aware methods or filters; avoid learning prejudicial domain-specific associations that do not generalize.
